accuracy.reason: All eight card objectives hold: acceptance/completion, actor acknowledgements, redelivery, atomic database deduplication, bounded retry, ordered effects, bounded buffering and retained-log scope. No universal durability or exactly-once guarantee; diagrams preserve these limits.

evidence.quote: That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

mechanisms.reason: Traces crash windows and atomic duplicate guard, per-entity serial effects and backlog arithmetic. Learner transfers every mechanism with exact supporting quotes.

evidence.quote: In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the receipt changes. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect. A separate check followed by a write can race or crash between steps.

coherence.reason: Receipt workflow carries from deferred result through acknowledgement, duplicates, failure, ordering and overload; log alternative reuses the same domain. Transactions/uniqueness are explicit prerequisites.

evidence.quote: Receives the message, saves the receipt and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker. A consumer acknowledgement lets the broker retire that delivery.

decisions.reason: Explains when synchronous completion is required, when deferral is acceptable, serial-lane cost, downstream headroom and queue versus log tradeoffs.

evidence.quote: The tradeoff includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog. A queue does not solve sustained overload.

clarity.reason: Terms are sufficient for the stated API/database audience. The log card introduces partition, group, offset, retention and ordering in a dense paragraph; explanation is usable but less paced than the earlier concrete crash sequence.

evidence.quote: If receipts and analytics each need every purchase event, a retained log such as Kafka supports separate consumer groups. A partition is an ordered slice of the log. Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions.

outcomes.reason: C1: API/broker/worker roles traced. C2: acceptance requires configured handoff and is not ready. C3: saved file/ready precedes consumer ack. C4: pending/ready/failed observable. C5: login decision required before access. C6: broker/worker/status operating cost; slides 1/2/8 support all.

C1: unacked credit redelivers. C2: early ack can lose credit. C3: stable ID/no-op repeats. C4: durable unique marker and balance change share transaction, no check/write gap. C5: database scope not universal exactly-once; exact slide 3 supports all.

C1: delayed finite retry budget. C2: invalid format isolated unchanged. C3: terminal DLQ with visible failure. C4: healthy work continues. C5: repair and check prior effects before deliberate replay; exact slide 4 supports all.

C1: old quantity 5 overwrites 2. C2: reception differs from completion. C3: per-item lane holds later updates through retries. C4: other IDs parallel. C5: hot-item throughput bottleneck; slide 5 supports all, including DLQ dependency handling.

C1: 120-80=40/s. C2: oldest-job age threatens completion promise. C3: bound workers for saturated store. C4: visible throttle/reject/defer. C5: finite storage/retention and sustained overload. C6: more workers only with worker bottleneck and downstream headroom; slide 6 supports all.

C1: queue divides jobs with possible repeats. C2: separate groups each consume and internal workers share partitions. C3: independent per-partition offsets. C4: offsets do not delete data. C5: replay only while required data retained. C6: partition order and no exactly-once external-effect promise; slide 7 and its diagram support all.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft async request-reply separates accepted work from result/status and delayed failure; lesson accurately makes client tolerance necessary.
RabbitMQ confirms and consumer acknowledgements are orthogonal; consumer ack retires delivery, not proof of arbitrary business effect. Diagram accurately separates boundaries.
AWS idempotent APIs requires stable caller tokens and atomic token/mutation recording; RabbitMQ confirms documents unacked redelivery. Database-only scope avoids an external-effect guarantee.
Microsoft Retry distinguishes transient from persistent failures with bounded delay; Competing Consumers documents poison/DLQ isolation. Replay must still respect already-applied effects.
Microsoft Competing Consumers warns about order and describes single-consumer session grouping; lesson correctly demonstrates ordered delivery can still produce unordered concurrent effects.
Microsoft load leveling warns concurrent downstream overload and buffering limits. Backlog arithmetic and bounded admission follow from arrivals exceeding completions.

Kafka Design describes independent consumer groups, partition positions, rewind, retention and cooperation needed for external exactly-once effects. Queue/log diagram preserves shared-work versus independent-history distinction.
Microsoft async request-reply supports status-based deferred work; caller-required authorization cannot safely be used before completion. Added status/operation burdens are explicit.
